title: Number of Valid Words in a Sentence
statement:
The string `sentence` is made only of lowercase letters, digits, hyphens (`-`), the punctuation marks `!`, `.` and `,`, and spaces. Splitting it at spaces gives its tokens: the maximal runs of non-space characters (tokens may be separated by several spaces, and there is at least one token). A token counts as a valid word when all of these hold:

- It contains no digit.
- It has at most one hyphen, and a hyphen must have a lowercase letter directly before it and directly after it (`a-b` is fine; `-ab`, `ab-` and `a-!` are not).
- It has at most one punctuation mark, and that mark must be the token's last character (`ab,` and `!` are fine; `a!b` and `c.,` are not).

Return how many tokens of `sentence` are valid words.
constraints: sentence contains only lowercase English letters, digits, ' ', '-', '!', '.' and ','
sentence has at least one token

examples.name: Example 3
input: alice and  bob are playing stone-game10

tests.name: Test 9
input: a b c d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z

notes:
## Intuition

Each token is judged on its own, and every rule is local: a digit anywhere fails, a hyphen depends on its two neighbours and on how many hyphens came before, and a punctuation mark only needs to be last. So split the sentence into tokens and scan each one once. (A regular expression such as `^([a-z]+(-[a-z]+)?)?[!.,]?$` expresses the same rules and makes a good cross-check.)

## Approach

1. Split `sentence` at single spaces and skip the empty pieces that runs of spaces produce.
2. For each `token`, start with `valid = true` and `hyphens = 0`, and scan its characters while it is still valid.
3. A digit makes the token invalid.
4. A hyphen increases `hyphens`; it is fine only if it is the first one and both neighbours are letters (`between`).
5. A punctuation mark is fine only at the last index. That also limits it to one mark: a second one could not be last too.
6. Letters are always fine. If the token survives the scan, add 1 to `count`.

## Example 1, step by step

`"cat and  dog".split(' ')` gives `["cat", "and", "", "dog"]`. The empty piece from the double space is skipped. `"cat"`, `"and"` and `"dog"` contain only letters, so each scan leaves `valid = true` and `count` becomes 3.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n), where n is `sentence.length`: each character is looked at once.
- Space: O(n) for the split pieces.

## Pitfalls

- Several spaces in a row produce empty tokens; they are not words and must not be counted.
- A hyphen at either end of a token, or next to a punctuation mark (`a-!`), fails: both neighbours must be letters.
- A lone punctuation mark such as `!` is a valid word.
- Two hyphens fail even when each one is between letters (`a-b-c`).

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count` | number of valid words found so far |
| `token` | the current piece of the sentence |
| `valid` | whether `token` still passes every rule |
| `hyphens` | hyphens seen so far in `token` |
| `i`, `ch` | position and character being checked |
| `between` | whether the hyphen has a letter on each side |
